title: Knowing what drives China in SCS

Historical narrative grounding: China's 'long and glorious history' set against its mid-1800s to mid-1900s 'harrowing decay' (the 'century of humiliation' framing)
Cultural premise: 'to the traditional Chinese, losing face is worse than losing life'
Geographic-strategic constraint: China surrounded by unfriendly neighbors versus US-friendly-neighbors-plus-oceans buffer
Geopolitical pressure: US Indo-Pacific pivot, Asia Reassurance Initiative Act of 2018, the Quad (US/Japan/Australia/India), NATO's recent 'systemic challenges' communique on China
Domestic-political driver: leadership teaches 1.3 billion people that SCS is cherished inheritance; failure to occupy and protect it leads to purge, dethronement, and banishment for treason

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that effective adversary analysis requires knowing what drives the other side -- and asks why China is so aggressive in owning almost the entire South China Sea (SCS) and the East China Sea (ECS). He grounds his answer in four drivers. First, civilizational pride: China claims a long history rivaling Egypt's pharaohs and Greece's Olympic gods, set against a 'harrowing decay' from the mid-1800s to mid-1900s of one-sided treaties and cruel treatment of nationals, with the cultural premise that 'to the traditional Chinese, losing face is worse than losing life.' Second, contested historical title: the WWII Japanese occupation of Paracels and Spratlys; the 1945 Cairo and Potsdam Declarations; Kuomintang acceptance of the Japanese surrender; Mao's 1950 takeover of the Paracels and Spratlys after driving the KMT to Taiwan; North Vietnam's wartime relinquishment of claims (later reversed by united Vietnam); the 1974 expulsion of South Vietnam from Shanhu Island; and the current feature-occupation count (Vietnam ~29, Philippines 11, China 7, Malaysia 6, Taiwan 2, Brunei 1). The Arbitral Award gives the Philippines sovereign rights over the maritime domain but not territorial sovereignty over land features and their territorial seas, while China, Vietnam, and others anchor their claims in history, discovery, occupation, control, and treaty-cession. Third, geographic constriction: China is the world's second-largest economy (soon largest), with the biggest standing military and a nuclear arsenal, lunar astronauts and a space station, yet is surrounded by unfriendly neighbors -- Russia on the north, former Soviet republics on the west, India and Vietnam on the south, and Japan, South Korea, and the 'renegade province' of Taiwan (all three with US defense agreements) on the east -- with only North Korea, Cambodia, and Mongolia as dependable neighbors; while the US enjoys friendly neighbors (Canada north, Mexico south) and two ocean buffers plus Caribbean control. China can expand only through the ECS and SCS, which serve as economic lifelines (sea lanes), security buffers (first line of defense against US military adventurism), and offensive corridors (passageway for nuclear submarines to the Pacific and Indian Oceans). Fourth, perceived US-led encirclement: the US Indo-Pacific pivot abetted by the Asia Reassurance Initiative Act of 2018, the Quad alliance with Australia, Japan, and India, and NATO's recent communique (under Biden's prodding) labeling China a 'systemic challenge.' Finally, domestic-political constraint: Chinese leadership has taught its 1.3 billion people that the SCS is cherished inheritance, and any leader who fails to occupy and protect it will surely be 'purged, dethroned, and banished for treason and disloyalty' -- making concession politically impossible for Beijing.
